title: AI with Spreadsheets: privacy & checking answers
goal: Decide what's safe to paste into an AI tool, swap names and phone numbers for IDs, and check an AI's numbers against your own sheet before you trust them.

steps.text:
An AI tool can explain a formula, clean a list or summarise sales in seconds. It's a fast helper, with **two rules**.

**Rule 1: share only what you must.** Whatever you paste or upload leaves your computer. Check your workplace's policy, and read the tool's privacy settings: free and business versions often treat your data differently.

**Rule 2: check every number.** An AI sounds just as sure when it's wrong.

Here's a customer sheet. To count orders per city, the AI needs only ==C== and ==D==. The names and phone numbers in ==A== and ==B== can stay home.

steps.prompt: Some columns point straight at a real person. Click the **column letter** of the one column here that would let a stranger phone a customer, then press [[Enter]].
steps.wrongFeedback: Not that one. Look for the column of digits someone could dial: that's **Phone**, column C.
clues: The letters A, B, C, D sit in the grey bar above the first row.

steps.prompt: You want an AI to help write a formula for this staff sheet. What's the **safest** thing to paste into the chat?
options: The header row and 3 made-up sample rows
The whole sheet, names and salaries included
Only the salary column, no names
steps.explain: The AI needs the **shape** of your sheet (column names and the kind of value in each), not the real data. A made-up row like “Asha, Sales, 30000” teaches it just as well.
wrongFeedback: Real names beside real salaries is exactly the data that shouldn't leave your workplace.
In a small team a salary on its own can still point to one person. Made-up rows are safer.
clues: Ask: does the AI need the real values, or only the layout?

steps.prompt:
Before sharing sales by customer, replace the real names with IDs.

In ==A2:A4== type **C1**, **C2**, **C3** (press [[Enter]] after each). Then type **hidden** over the three phone numbers in ==C2:C4==.

Keep your own private list of who C1, C2 and C3 are.
steps.explain: The orders stay, so the AI can still total and compare them, but nobody can tell who C2 is without your private list. To swap a name everywhere at once, [[Ctrl]] + [[H]] opens Find & Replace.

wrongFeedback.empty: There are still real names or phone numbers left. Fill all six cells: three IDs in column A, three “hidden” in column C.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Check the spelling. Column A should read C1, C2, C3 in order, and column C should say hidden.

clues: Click ==A2==, type C1, Enter, then C2, Enter, then C3. Do the phone cells the same way.

steps.prompt: You **hide** column C (Phone) and then upload the file to an AI tool. Is the phone data still shared?
options: No, hidden columns are left out
Yes, hidden columns still travel with the file
No, as long as the sheet has a password
steps.explain: Hiding only changes what you see on screen; every number is still inside the file. Make a **copy**, delete the private columns there, and upload that. Sheet protection isn't a lock on the data either.
wrongFeedback: Hiding is cosmetic. Anyone who opens the file can unhide the column.
A protect-sheet password stops editing, not reading. Delete the data from the copy instead.
clues: Think about what happens if the person you send it to clicks “Unhide”.

steps.prompt:
An AI tool says: “Your six items cost **2,320** in total.” Looking at the sheet, the biggest cost is 250.

Without calculating anything exactly: can 2,320 be right?
options: No: six items of at most 250 can't pass 1,500
Yes, AI tools are good at sums
Yes, if the prices include tax
steps.explain: 6 × 250 = 1,500 is the most the column could ever reach. A rough size check takes five seconds and catches many AI slips. Next you'll find out what really happened.
wrongFeedback: AI tools can slip on arithmetic, especially on longer tables. Never assume.
Even with tax, 1,500 plus a little is nowhere near 2,320.
clues: What's the biggest total six numbers of 250 or less could make?

steps.prompt: Now find the real number. Click ==D2== and total the six costs (`B2:B7`) yourself.
steps.explain: **1,160.** The AI's 2,320 is exactly double: it most likely added the **Total row** (`B8`) into the total. A total sitting inside the range is one of the most common AI and human slips.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use `SUM` on the six cost cells.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Add only the six items, `B2:B7`. Leave out the Total row.
wrongFeedback.missingReference: Use the six costs, `B2:B7`, so the check is really yours.

clues: `=SUM(B2:B7)`: first item to last item, nothing else.

steps.prompt: An AI summary says: “**North** sold **1,200** this week.” Check it. Type a formula in ==D2== that gives North's real total.
steps.explain: **750**, not 1,200. The AI's figure is 750 plus South's 450, so it probably grabbed a wrong row. One `SUMIF` is all it takes to catch that.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Add up only the rows where the region is North: that's a job for `SUMIF`.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: North appears three times (300, 250, 200). Add only those rows.

clues: `=SUMIF(range to look in, "North", range to add)`.

steps.prompt: The AI says: “**4** orders were **over** 500.” Check it. In ==D2== count the orders with an amount **over** 500.
steps.explain: **3.** The AI's 4 counted the order of exactly 500. “Over 500” leaves 500 out; “500 or more” would keep it. Wording like “over”, “at least” and “up to” is where AI answers slip most.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Count the amounts that pass a test. `COUNTIF` does that.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: You're probably counting the 500 as well. “Over 500” means 501 and up, so use `>` and not `>=`.

steps.prompt: An AI gives you a total that looks believable. What's the **best** way to check it?
options: Reply “are you sure?” and see if it changes
Trust it if it explains how it got there
Recalculate that number yourself with a formula on the sheet
steps.explain: Your own `SUM`, `COUNTIF` or `SUMIF` on the real cells is an independent check. Do it for every number that goes into a report, a bill or an email.
wrongFeedback: Asking again isn't a check. It may flip a right answer to a wrong one, or repeat the same mistake.
A neat explanation can sit on top of a wrong number. Recalculate; don't judge the story.
clues: Which option uses the actual cells, not the AI's word?

steps.prompt: An AI report says: “The **average score for Mumbai** is **78**.” What is it really? Put your answer in ==D2==.
steps.explain: **74.** The AI's 78 is the average of **all six** scores. It answered for the whole sheet, not for Mumbai. Always check that the AI used the filter you asked for.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: 78 is the average of every branch. Average only the three Mumbai rows.
wrongFeedback.missingReference: Look at both columns: branch in `A2:A7`, scores in `B2:B7`.

clues: Which rows say Mumbai? Average just their scores.
